narrative.text: Lists the abbreviations used in the Swaziland case study, from antenatal care and antiretroviral therapy to UN agencies and local HIV organizations, and begins the opening section on making the case for Prongs 1 and 2. Entries cover health services, surveys, networks of people living with HIV and peer-education programmes.

Defines the distinction between linkages and integration of sexual and reproductive health and HIV services, and notes a shift in global attention from preventing mother-to-child transmission alone towards recognizing links between maternal health, HIV and child survival under the Millennium Development Goals.

Explains the global commitment to eliminate new HIV infections among children by 2015 while keeping mothers alive, built on four prongs of comprehensive programming integrated with sexual and reproductive health. It highlights growing attention to the first two prongs, preventing HIV in women and preventing unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV. Tables set out the prongs and associated interventions such as family planning, blood safety, stigma reduction and prevention of gender-based violence.

Presents a table of Swaziland's vital statistics, including population, life expectancy, fertility, adult HIV prevalence, estimated numbers living with HIV, AIDS deaths, contraceptive prevalence, skilled birth attendance and PMTCT coverage. It introduces the case study of services supporting Prongs 1 and 2.

Describes the background to Swaziland's HIV epidemic, noting the world's highest adult HIV prevalence, very low life expectancy and a high proportion of pregnant women living with HIV. It closes with a statement by the Prime Minister to the UN General Assembly committing the country to reduce new infections among children to zero by 2015.

Profiles the case study sites in Swaziland, starting with the Family Life Association of Swaziland and its youth-friendly clinics offering integrated sexual and reproductive health and HIV services, alongside other service providers mapped across the country. It then documents promising practices addressing Prong 1, preventing HIV among women, and Prong 2, preventing unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV. The section covers community outreach, peer education, counselling, family planning and linked referral services. It ends with a checklist of questions that facilities can use to assess whether they provide these services and have built them into standard operating procedures.

Lists key resources on linking sexual and reproductive health and HIV, including a linkages resource pack and the 2011–2015 strategic framework on preventing HIV and unintended pregnancies, each with a short description. Most are produced by UN agencies, IPPF and the Inter-Agency Task Team.

The endnotes for the Swaziland case study on linking sexual and reproductive health and HIV, citing mainly UN agency, IPPF and Inter-Agency Task Team publications. Sources include the Global Plan, strategic frameworks, linkage assessment tools and Swazi national HIV training materials.

The front matter of a 2011 WHO, UNFPA, UNAIDS and IPPF case study from Swaziland on linking sexual and reproductive health with HIV/AIDS services, in support of the Global Plan to eliminate new HIV infections among children. It contains the title pages, copyright and disclaimer notice with publisher contact details, acknowledgements of Swazi and international partner organizations and main contributors, and the table of contents.
